entries.topicDescription: Fragment lifecycle, communication, and management within Activities and Navigation.

tips.title: Use the Fragment Result API instead of direct references between Fragments for communication
tips.content:
Having one Fragment hold a direct reference to another (or to its host
Activity cast to a specific interface) tightly couples them and breaks
easily during navigation changes or configuration changes, when Fragment
instances are recreated.

The Fragment Result API lets a Fragment set a result keyed by a request
key, and another Fragment listen for it via the FragmentManager — neither
Fragment needs a direct reference to the other, and it correctly survives
Fragment recreation since it's coordinated through the FragmentManager
rather than a direct object reference.

tips.title: Observe with viewLifecycleOwner inside a Fragment, not the Fragment itself
tips.content:
A Fragment can outlive its view: when it goes on the back stack its view is destroyed but the Fragment object stays. If you collect a Flow with the Fragment's own lifecycle, the collector keeps running while the view is gone and a new one is added each time the view is recreated, causing duplicate updates and touching a null binding.

viewLifecycleOwner is tied to the view, so collectors start and stop with it. Use it for every observer that updates the UI.

tips.title: childFragmentManager, parentFragmentManager or the Activity's manager?
tips.content:
A Fragment has more than one FragmentManager and the choice matters. childFragmentManager manages fragments hosted inside this Fragment (nested fragments). parentFragmentManager is the manager this Fragment itself is attached to, which is where siblings can be reached. requireActivity().supportFragmentManager is the Activity-level manager.

Use childFragmentManager for nested content and for results between a parent and its children, parentFragmentManager for results between siblings, and avoid reaching for the Activity's manager from inside a Fragment.

tips.title: Use a FragmentFactory when a Fragment needs constructor arguments
tips.content:
The system recreates Fragments after configuration changes or process death by calling their no-argument constructor, so a Fragment with a constructor parameter would crash on restore unless you tell the FragmentManager how to build it. A FragmentFactory does that: it receives the class name and returns a fully constructed instance.

Set the factory on the FragmentManager before super.onCreate, so it is in place when the system restores fragments. (With Hilt, @AndroidEntryPoint fragments get their dependencies injected without a custom factory.)
